newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Colgate ruling seen as example for Mercosur.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Colgate ruling seen as example for Mercosur.

text.p: A ruling by Brazil's anti- trust watchdog allowing Colgate-Palmolive to buy out oral hygiene firm Anakol is a signal that the Mercosur trade bloc takes competition seriously, said a member of the agency.

Councillor Lucia Helena Salgado e Silva told Reuters it also showed that the Administrative Economic Defence Council (Cade) had matured and would start looking at anti-trust cases with more emphasis on international law and with greater complexity.
"The decision of Cade is a signal to international investors that Mercosur is not a monopolistic market and that competition is important," she said.
Cade ruled late Wednesday in favor of the buyout, but set conditions to stop Colgate snapping up a 77 percent share of the Brazilian toothpaste market overnight.

Colgate must either refrain from selling the Kolynos toothpaste brand in Brazil for four years, licence it to a third party over a 20-year period, or sell the brand to a competitor with a less than one percent market share.

"The ruling represents a change in Cade in that we no longer want to adopt a simplistic position of yes or no," Silva said. She said the decision was taken in close consultation with international anti-cartel norms and with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
"We are on the path to becoming civilized," she said.

The ruling was welcomed by the U.S. personal hygiene giant, which purchased Anakol in 1995. The Brazilian operation accounts for $760 million of the total buyout and the Kolynos brand, with a 50 percent market share in Brazil, is the icing on the cake.

"We are satisfied with the approval of the investment we made in our most important business area, oral hygiene, in the biggest and most powerful economy of Latin America," Colgate administrative board president Reuben Mark said in a statement.
Mark, speaking in New York, but whose comments were distributed in Brazil, said Colgate would reply to Cade within the 30-day limit and was hopeful about satisfying Cade's conditions.

Silva said the ruling would not in any way affect Colgate's other business plans for Latin America, especially its intention to export Brazilian-made Kolynos to other countries in the region and also other emerging markets.
"The decision does not affect any other plans of the company," she said.

Silva noted that the buyout not only gave Colgate a 77 percent share of the Brazilian toothpaste market, but also 75 percent of all of Mercosur, grouping Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. Being the biggest market of the four, the ruling in Brazil would naturally have an impact on Colgate's activities in the other countries, she said.
Cade has come under the spotlight in recent months with rumoured attempts by the government to exert greater influence on its rulings. But Silva said the body was wholly independent.
